blocks.html: In Check Your Writing you read your work over before you shared it. Longer writing needs more than one check at the end. Most writers move through five stages, and they often go back to an earlier one when they learn something new.

head: Stage
What you do
The question it answers
rows: Choose and narrow a topic, gather ideas, plan
Write it all the way through, without stopping to polish
Can I get it all down?
Add, cut, move and replace ideas, sentences and paragraphs
Does it say what I mean, in the best order?
Fix grammar, punctuation, spelling and format
Share the clean copy with its readers
blocks.cap: The five stages of the writing process.

blocks.html: Writers prewrite, draft, revise, edit and publish. Revising changes what the writing says and how it is organized; editing fixes the sentences. The stages loop: a writer who finds a gap while revising goes back to gather more ideas.

Doing everything at once is slow and frustrating. If you fix commas while you are still deciding what to say, you may polish a sentence you later cut. Separate stages let you think about one kind of problem at a time: ideas first, then order, then sentences.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: Prewriting: brainstorm and plan
Drafting: write it all down
Revising: improve ideas and order
Editing: fix the sentences
Publishing: share the final copy
opts.title: Put the stages in their usual order.

blocks.cap: Tap two cards to swap them, or use the arrows. Then Check.

blocks.title: Which stage is it?
blocks.q: Lena moves her best reason from the middle of her essay to the end, so it is the last thing her reader remembers. Which stage is she in?
steps: She is not fixing a comma or a spelling, so this is not editing.
She is changing the order of her ideas.
Changing ideas and order is revising.
blocks.a: Revising.

blocks.title: Revising or editing?
blocks.q: Omar changes “there dog” to “their dog.” Which stage is that?
steps: He changed one word to the correct spelling.
The idea and the order are the same as before.
Fixing a word or a mark in a sentence is editing.
blocks.a: Editing.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Cut a paragraph that wanders off the topic.
cards.why: Cutting an idea changes what the piece says.

cards.text: Add a capital letter to a name.
cards.why: A capital is a fix inside a sentence.

cards.text: Add an example to support a point.
cards.why: New support is a change to the ideas.

cards.text: Fix a run-on sentence.
cards.why: Sentence errors are fixed while editing.

cards.text: Move the strongest reason to the end.
Change “alot” to “a lot.”

blocks.cap: Sort each change: revising (ideas and order) or editing (sentences).

blocks.html: Thinking revising means fixing spelling. A paper with every comma right can still be missing its best example or have its paragraphs in a confusing order. Check: after you revise, could a reader tell that the ideas changed? If only the commas changed, you edited.

Writing on a computer blurs the stages, since you can fix things as you go. That is fine, as long as you still make a separate pass for ideas and a separate pass for errors. The Mother Tongue books on this site teach the same habit: plan, write, then read it over with fresh eyes.

blocks.html: Every piece of writing starts with two questions from the writing process: Why am I writing? (the purpose) and Who will read it? (the audience). The answers decide what you include and how you say it.

items: To inform or explain: a report on how bees make honey, directions to a party.
To persuade: a letter asking the principal for a longer lunch period.
To tell a story or entertain: a story about the day the power went out.
To express feelings or connect: a thank-you note, a journal entry.

blocks.html: Purpose is why you write; audience is who reads. Choose your details, your words and your tone to fit both: give the reader what they need to know, in a voice that suits them.

A reader can’t stop you to ask a question. A good writer imagines the reader and answers their questions on the page. Your best friend already knows your dog’s name; the town council doesn’t. A tone that is friendly in a text to a cousin can sound careless in a letter to a business.

blocks.title: Same news, two audiences
blocks.q: Jada’s soccer team won the city final. How should her message change for her grandmother and for the school newsletter?
steps: Purpose for both: to share the news (inform), and for Grandma also to connect.
Grandma knows Jada but not the team. Jada can be warm and personal: “We won! I blocked a shot in the last minute.”
Newsletter readers don’t know the players. They need the facts: who, what, when, the score.
Newsletter tone: clear and even: “The seventh-grade team beat Riverside 2–1 in Saturday’s city final.”
blocks.a: Personal and warm for Grandma; factual and complete for the newsletter.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: A flyer listing the times and place of the book fair.
A letter asking the city to put a crosswalk near school.
A tale about a raccoon that sneaks into a campsite.
Directions for feeding the class fish over the weekend.
A speech urging classmates to vote for a new club.
cards.why: It tries to change what readers do.

cards.text: An account of the funniest thing that happened on the field trip.

blocks.cap: Sort each piece by its main purpose.

blocks.html: Writing only for the teacher, who already knows the subject, so you skip facts a real reader would need. Check: hand your draft to someone who knows nothing about the topic. Every question they ask marks a spot where the writing assumed too much.
Many pieces have more than one purpose. A review informs (what the movie is about) and persuades (see it, or skip it). Name the main purpose, and let it lead.

blocks.html: Once you know your purpose and audience, you need something to say. Prewriting is the stage where you gather ideas and choose a topic small enough to cover well.

items: Brainstorm or list: write every idea that comes, fast, without judging.
Freewrite: write without stopping for five or ten minutes, then circle the best lines.
Cluster (a web): write the topic in a circle and connect related ideas around it.
Ask questions: who, what, when, where, why and how.

blocks.html: Gather ideas first, then narrow the topic until it fits the space you have. A two-page paper needs a topic you can explain with real detail in two pages.

A topic that is too big forces you to say a little about everything, so the writing stays vague. A narrow topic leaves room for the specific facts, examples and details that make writing interesting and convincing.

blocks.title: Narrowing step by step
blocks.q: Narrow “sports” to a topic for a one-page paper.
steps: Sports: thousands of games across thousands of years. Far too big.
Basketball: still a whole history, rules and players.
The three-point line: one rule, but its whole history is still a lot for one page.
Why our school added a three-point line to its middle-school league: one change, one place, one page.
blocks.a: Why our school league added a three-point line.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: Animals
Pets
Dogs
Training a puppy
Teaching a puppy to sit
opts.title: Order these topics from biggest to smallest.

blocks.cap: Each topic sits inside the one before it. The last one fits a short paper.

blocks.title: Does it fit?
blocks.q: Which topic fits a one-paragraph answer: “The history of flight” or “How a paper airplane stays up”?
steps: The history of flight covers centuries and many inventors: a book, not a paragraph.
How a paper airplane stays up is one process you can explain in a few sentences.
blocks.a: “How a paper airplane stays up.”

blocks.html: Choosing a topic far too big for the length, like “the history of sports” in two pages. Test it: can you name the three or four specific points you would make? If each point is itself a big subject, narrow again.
Narrowing can go too far. “The color of my left shoelace” has nothing to explain. A good topic is small enough to cover well and big enough to be worth a reader’s time.

blocks.html: In Tell What It Is About you named the topic of a piece. A paragraph does the same in one sentence. The topic sentence states the paragraph’s main idea, usually right at the start, so the reader knows what every other sentence is there to support.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Owls are built to hunt in the dark.
Their large eyes gather what little light there is.
In many owls, one ear sits a little higher than the other, which helps them find a mouse by sound alone.
Soft edges on their feathers let them fly almost silently.
Few animals are as well made for the night.

blocks.cap: The topic sentence makes a point; every other sentence backs it up.

blocks.html: A topic sentence states the paragraph’s main idea: a topic plus what you will say about it. It is broad enough to cover the whole paragraph, and specific enough to need support.

Readers understand details faster when they know what the details are for. Strunk’s rule 9 (1918) puts it simply: “As a rule, begin each paragraph with a topic sentence.” The topic sentence is a promise; the rest of the paragraph keeps it.

blocks.title: Announcement or topic sentence?
blocks.q: Improve: “This paragraph is about owls.”
steps: It names the topic (owls) but says nothing about it.
Ask: what do I want to show about owls?
Add the point: owls are built to hunt in the dark.
blocks.a: “Owls are built to hunt in the dark.”

blocks.title: Too small to be the main idea
blocks.q: Could “Owls have soft edges on their feathers.” be the topic sentence of the owl paragraph above?
steps: It is true, but it is one detail.
It doesn’t cover the eyes or the ears.
A detail belongs in the body of the paragraph, supporting a bigger point.
blocks.a: No. It is a supporting detail, not the main idea.

blocks.html: Writing an announcement (“This paragraph is about dogs.” “I am going to tell you about…”) or a small detail as the topic sentence. Check: does it make a point about the topic, and does every other sentence in the paragraph fit under it?

items: Too broad: “Animals are interesting.” (Which ones? How?)
Too narrow: “An owl’s eye is shaped like a tube.” (One detail.)
Just right: “Owls are built to hunt in the dark.”

blocks.html: In stories and in some essays, a writer may hold the main idea back or leave it implied. For explaining and arguing, a clear topic sentence near the start is the dependable choice.

blocks.html: A topic sentence makes a point. The rest of the paragraph proves or explains it with supporting details.

head: Kind of support
Example for “Our town needs a dog park.”
rows: The town has 1,200 licensed dogs and no fenced place to run them.
Last spring, two loose dogs ran into traffic on Pine Street.
Dogs that get exercise bark less and sleep better.
The empty lot behind the library is flat, shady and already fenced on two sides.
blocks.cap: Four kinds of support for one topic sentence (an invented town).

blocks.html: Supporting details are facts, examples, reasons and details that show the main idea is true. Each one must connect to the topic sentence and add something new.

A reader has no reason to accept a point that stands alone. Details turn a claim into something the reader can see and check. They also keep the writing specific: “dogs ran into traffic on Pine Street” sticks in the mind; “it is unsafe” doesn’t.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Taking the bus to school saves families time and money.
Parents don’t have to sit in the morning line of cars.
Families who drive also pay for the gas for two trips a day.
For example, my neighbor started riding the bus and now has an extra half hour each morning.
The bus is a small change that pays off every day.

blocks.cap: Two reasons and an example support the topic sentence.

blocks.title: Support or restatement?
blocks.q: Topic sentence: “Tomatoes are easy to grow.” Which detail supports it: (a) “Growing tomatoes is not hard.” or (b) “A single plant in a sunny pot can produce fruit all summer.”
steps: (a) says the same thing as the topic sentence in other words. It adds nothing.
(b) gives a specific fact a reader can picture.
Support must add new information.

blocks.title: True but off the point
blocks.q: Same topic. Does “Tomatoes first grew wild in South America.” support it?
steps: It is a fact about tomatoes.
But it says nothing about whether they are easy to grow.
A detail can be true and still not support this point.
blocks.a: No. It is true but off the point.

blocks.html: Adding details that are true but off the point, or repeating the topic sentence in new words. Test each sentence with the question: does this help prove or explain the topic sentence, and does it say something new?

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), On Paragraphs
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Body Paragraphs (argument papers)

blocks.html: You know that supporting details must connect to the main idea. A paragraph has unity when every sentence does. One sentence that drifts can pull the reader off course.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Our school garden gives students a real science lab.
Students measure how fast bean plants grow in sun and in shade.
They test the soil to see which plants need more water.
The cafeteria serves tacos every Tuesday.
sentences.why: Tacos have nothing to do with the garden as a science lab.

sentences.text: Every harvest becomes a lesson in what worked and why.

blocks.cap: Tap the sentence that breaks the paragraph’s unity, then Check.

blocks.html: In a unified paragraph, every sentence supports the one main idea. A sentence about something else, even an interesting one, belongs in a different paragraph or nowhere.

Strunk’s rule 8 (1918) says, “Make the paragraph the unit of composition: one paragraph to each topic.” Readers use paragraphs to sort ideas. When a paragraph mixes two topics, the reader can’t tell which one matters, and the main idea gets weaker.

blocks.title: Find the drift
blocks.q: “(1) Penguins are excellent swimmers. (2) Their wings work like flippers. (3) Their bodies are shaped like torpedoes. (4) Some penguins live in warm places, such as the Galápagos. (5) They can stay underwater for several minutes.” Which sentence breaks the unity?
steps: The main idea: penguins are excellent swimmers.
Sentences 2, 3 and 5 explain how they swim.
Sentence 4 is about where penguins live, not how they swim.
blocks.a: Sentence 4.

blocks.title: Cut it or move it?
blocks.q: What should the writer do with the sentence about the Galápagos?
steps: It is a good fact, but about a different idea: where penguins live.
If the essay has a paragraph about penguin homes, move it there.
If not, cut it.
blocks.a: Move it to a paragraph about where penguins live, or cut it.

blocks.html: Keeping an interesting sentence that drifts from the main idea because it is fun or took effort to find. Check each sentence against the topic sentence, not against the sentence just before it: a paragraph can drift one small step at a time.

In Stay on Topic young writers learn the same idea with pictures. In longer writing, unity applies at two levels: each paragraph sticks to its topic sentence, and each paragraph sticks to the essay’s thesis.

blocks.html: A unified paragraph has the right sentences. Transitions show the reader how those sentences connect: which comes next in time, which adds to the last, which turns against it, which follows from it.

head: Relationship
Transitions
rows: first, next, then, later, meanwhile, finally
however, on the other hand, instead, still, in contrast
therefore, as a result, so, consequently
for example, for instance, in particular
in short, overall, in the end
blocks.cap: Transitions grouped by the relationship they signal.

blocks.html: Choose a transition for the relationship between two ideas: time, addition, contrast, cause and effect, or example. The wrong transition sends the reader the wrong signal.

Transitions are road signs. “However” tells the reader to expect a turn; “therefore” tells them a result is coming. When the sign matches the road, the reader follows easily. When it doesn’t, they stop and reread.

blocks.title: Choose the signal
blocks.q: “The library closes at six. ___, students who stay late at practice can’t check out books.” Which transition fits?
steps: The second idea is a result of the first: it closes early, so late students miss it.
Cause and effect: as a result, therefore, so.
“However” would signal a contrast, which isn’t there.
blocks.a: “As a result” (or “Therefore”).

blocks.title: A contrast
blocks.q: “Hamsters are easy to care for. ___, they sleep all day and are awake at night.”
steps: The second sentence is a drawback, against the first.
That is a contrast: however, on the other hand, still.
blocks.a: “However.”

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: ; as a result,
joins.make: The bus was late; as a result, we missed the first bell.
joins.why: Missing the bell is a result of the late bus.

joins.label: ; however,
joins.make: The bus was late; however, we missed the first bell.
joins.why: However signals a contrast, but these ideas agree.

joins.label: ; for example,
joins.make: The bus was late; for example, we missed the first bell.
joins.why: The second idea is not an example of the first.

blocks.cap: Try each transition and see whether its signal fits.

blocks.html: Using a transition that signals the wrong relationship (“however” where the idea continues), or starting every sentence with one. Check by reading the two sentences with the transition’s meaning spelled out: “however” means “but in contrast.” Does that make sense? And let some sentences connect without a word, through repeated key terms.
When a transition like however joins two complete sentences, put a semicolon or a period before it and a comma after it. A comma alone makes a comma splice.

Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Revising for Cohesion

blocks.html: Transitions connect sentences; order decides which sentence comes where. Choose an order that matches what you are writing about, so the reader can follow without effort.

head: Order
Use it for
Signal words
rows: describing a room, a map, a scene
above, next to, across, at the back
blocks.cap: Four common ways to order details.

blocks.html: Arrange details in an order the reader can follow: by time, by place, by importance, or by comparison. Pick the order that fits the subject, then keep to it.

A reader builds a picture as they read. Steps in time order let them follow along; a room described left to right lets them “walk” through it. Ideas in the order the writer happened to think of them make the reader do the sorting.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: First, rinse the rice until the water runs clear.
Next, put one cup of rice and two cups of water in a pot.
Then bring the water to a boil.
After that, cover the pot and simmer for about eighteen minutes.
Finally, let it rest for five minutes before serving.
opts.title: Put the steps for cooking rice in time order.

blocks.cap: A process paragraph uses time order, with time transitions.

blocks.title: Order by importance
blocks.q: A student lists three reasons for a longer lunch period: students eat more slowly and digest better; there would be time to visit the library; many students now can’t finish eating at all. In what order should they go?
steps: Rank by importance: not finishing lunch is the most serious problem.
Many writers build up: least important first, most important last, so the paragraph ends strong.
So: library time, then eating slowly, then not finishing at all.
blocks.a: Library time → eating slowly → students who can’t finish (strongest last).

blocks.title: Which order fits?
blocks.q: What order fits a paragraph describing a bedroom?
steps: A description of a place is spatial.
Move the reader’s eye one way: door to window, or floor to ceiling.
blocks.a: Spatial order (place).

blocks.html: Listing details in the order you thought of them. Check: could you name the order you used (time, place, importance, comparison)? If not, choose one and rearrange.

For importance, both directions work: strongest first grabs a busy reader; strongest last leaves the best point in their mind. Choose on purpose. First, Next, Then, Last introduced time order for younger writers.

Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Revising for Cohesion

blocks.html: Once a paragraph’s details are in a clear order, it needs an ending. A concluding sentence tells the reader the point is finished and leaves them with the main idea.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Walking to school has real benefits for students.
A fifteen-minute walk gives students exercise before class.
Walkers arrive awake and ready to listen.
Walking with friends also gives them time to talk before the day starts.
A short walk is an easy way to start the school day strong.

blocks.cap: The concluding sentence returns to the main idea in new words.

blocks.html: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph: it restates the main idea in new words, sums up the support, or states a result. It doesn’t copy the topic sentence, and it doesn’t start a new idea.

Strunk’s rule 9 (1918) says to end a paragraph “in conformity with the beginning”: the last sentence “either emphasizes the thought of the topic sentence or states some important consequence.” The reader leaves the paragraph knowing exactly what it showed.

blocks.title: Three kinds of endings
blocks.q: Write a concluding sentence for a paragraph whose topic sentence is “Bats help farmers.”
steps: Restate in new words: “Bats are a farmer’s quiet allies.”
Sum up the support: “By eating pests and spreading seeds, bats save crops.”
State a result: “Protecting bats can mean bigger harvests.”
blocks.a: Any of the three works; each returns to the idea that bats help farmers.

blocks.title: What’s wrong with this ending?
blocks.q: Topic sentence: “Bats help farmers.” Ending: “Also, some bats live for more than thirty years.”
steps: “Also” signals one more point, not an ending.
How long bats live is a new idea, unrelated to farming.
A new idea at the end leaves the reader expecting more.
blocks.a: It starts a new idea instead of closing the main one.

blocks.html: Copying the topic sentence word for word, or bringing in a new idea at the very end. Check: cover the topic sentence and read your last sentence. It should point back to the same idea, in different words.

Not every paragraph needs a formal concluding sentence. In a longer essay, the last sentence of a body paragraph often links to the next paragraph instead. Short stand-alone paragraphs, like answers on a test, benefit most from a clear close.

blocks.html: You learned the shape of a story in A Problem and a Fix, and how to keep events in time order. A narrative uses both: it tells events in order, from a point of view, with characters, a setting, a conflict and a resolution.

head: Part
What it does
Example
rows: the people (or animals) in the story
a crowded county fair, a hot August evening
the problem the character must face
his sister lets go of his hand in the crowd
he searches the rides, then the food tents
he hears her laugh at the goat pen
he finds her feeding a goat, and never lets go again that night
blocks.cap: The parts of a narrative.

blocks.html: A narrative has characters, a setting, a conflict that builds to a turning point, and a resolution, told from a point of view (first person: “I”; third person: “he,” “she,” “they”). Its best moments are scenes the reader can see and hear.

People remember stories better than lists. A conflict gives the reader a question (will Marcus find her?) that pulls them forward. A scene with dialogue and detail lets the reader live the moment instead of hearing about it.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: Marcus held his sister’s hand at the gate of the fair.
At the ticket booth, he let go to count his money.
When he turned around, she was gone.
He searched the rides, then the food tents, his heart pounding.
Then he heard a giggle from the goat pen.
She was feeding a goat a handful of hay, perfectly happy.
opts.title: Put the story in order.

blocks.cap: Setting and characters, the conflict, rising action, the turning point and the resolution.

blocks.title: Summary or scene?
blocks.q: Turn this summary into a scene: “Marcus looked everywhere and was worried.”
steps: Ask: what did he do, see, hear and say?
Show the search with actions and details.
Add a line of dialogue to make it a moment.
blocks.a: “Marcus pushed past a stroller and climbed onto a bench. ‘Ellie!’ he shouted. Nothing but music and the smell of fried dough.”

blocks.html: Summarizing events (“then this happened, then that happened”) instead of building a scene the reader can see. Check your draft for one moment that matters most and slow it down: actions, a line of dialogue, one sharp detail. Keep the quick summary for the parts in between.
A personal narrative tells a true story from your own life, in first person. Purdue OWL’s narrative essay guide notes that it should still make a point: what the experience meant or taught.

blocks.html: A narrative comes alive in its scenes. One tool for scenes is showing: instead of naming a feeling, you give the reader the actions, words and details that let them feel it.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.del: Ana was very nervous before her piano recital.
segments.ins: Before her recital, Ana wiped her palms on her skirt for the third time and counted the people in the front row.
segments.why: Actions and details let the reader see the nerves.

blocks.cap: From telling to showing.

blocks.html: Show the moments that matter with action, dialogue and sensory details. Tell (summarize) when you need to move quickly through time or give simple facts. Good writing does both.

When you write “she was nervous,” the reader accepts the label but feels nothing. When you show sweaty palms and counting faces, the reader figures out the feeling for themselves, and that small act of figuring makes the moment real to them.

blocks.title: Show a feeling
blocks.q: Show, don’t tell: “Theo was angry.”
steps: What does anger look like? A slammed door, a short answer, a red face.
What might Theo say?
Combine one action, one detail, one line.
blocks.a: “Theo dropped his backpack so hard the zipper cracked. ‘Fine,’ he said, without looking up.”

blocks.title: When telling is the right choice
blocks.q: A story jumps from June to the first day of school. Should the writer show every day of summer?
steps: Nothing in those weeks matters to the story.
Showing each day would bury the important scenes.
A sentence of telling moves the reader forward.
blocks.a: No. Tell it: “The rest of the summer passed quietly.”

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: The dog was happy to see us.
The dog spun in circles, tail thumping the door.
It was a cold morning.
Frost crunched under our boots, and our breath hung in the air.
Grandpa was tired.
Grandpa lowered himself into the chair with a long sigh.

blocks.cap: Sort each sentence: does it show or tell?

items: Action: what the character does with hands, feet, face.
Dialogue: what they say, and how they say it.
Senses: what the character sees, hears, smells, tastes or touches.
Thoughts: a quick line of what goes through their mind.
Telling: a sentence that skips ahead or sums up when nothing important happens.

blocks.html: Naming every feeling (“She was scared. He was sad.”) where actions would show it, or the opposite mistake: believing you must never tell. A story that shows every moment is slow and tiring. Check: show the important moments; tell the bridges between them.

blocks.html: Descriptive writing uses showing to paint a person, place or thing so clearly that the reader can picture it. It relies on precise words and the five senses, arranged in a clear order.

items: Precise nouns: not “a bird” but “a blue jay.”
Strong verbs: not “walked slowly” but “shuffled.”
Sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
A clear order: near to far, left to right, or the most striking detail first.

blocks.html: Describe with precise nouns, strong verbs and sensory details, in a clear order. One exact word usually beats three general ones.

General words make the reader do the imagining, and every reader imagines something different. Specific words put your picture in their head. Strunk’s rule 12 (1918) says it plainly: “Use definite, specific, concrete language.”

blocks.name: wr-revise

opts.before: The big, huge, giant tree made a noise in the wind.
opts.after: The old oak groaned in the wind.

blocks.cap: Step through the revision: a precise noun and a strong verb replace a pile of adjectives.

blocks.title: Choose the precise word
blocks.q: Revise: “The dog ate the food fast.”
steps: Which dog? A beagle.
Which verb shows how it ate? Gulped, wolfed, gobbled.
Which food? A bowl of kibble.
blocks.a: “The beagle wolfed down his kibble.”

blocks.title: Use more than sight
blocks.q: Add two senses to: “The kitchen on Thanksgiving.”
steps: Smell: roasting turkey and cinnamon.
Sound: pots clanging, a timer buzzing.
Put them in one sentence.
blocks.a: “The kitchen smelled of roasting turkey and cinnamon, and a timer buzzed over the clang of pots.”

blocks.html: Stacking adjectives (“the big, huge, giant tree”) instead of choosing one precise noun or verb. Words that mean the same thing don’t add detail; they add length. Check each adjective: does it tell the reader something new? If two say the same thing, keep the better one, or find a noun that does the job alone.

The Words for the Five Senses topic in First Writing starts this skill. Description also helps outside stories: a science report that says “the solution turned cloudy and pale yellow” is more useful than “it changed.”

blocks.html: Stories and descriptions let readers experience something. Expository writing explains or informs: how a volcano forms, what a word means, why leaves change color. It builds on everything you know about paragraphs, from topic sentences to concluding sentences.
Expository writing explains or informs with facts, definitions, examples and clear steps, in a neutral voice. Its job is for the reader to understand, not to agree.

Readers of expository writing want to learn, and they trust a writer who sticks to what can be shown. Opinions slipped into an explanation make the reader wonder which parts are facts, so the whole piece becomes less useful.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Leaves change color in autumn because trees stop making chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll is the green substance leaves use to make food from sunlight.
As days get shorter, the tree breaks the chlorophyll down.
Yellow and orange colors that were there all along begin to show.
In some trees, new red colors also form in the leaves.
The bright colors of fall are the leaf’s last stage before it drops.

blocks.cap: An expository paragraph: each sentence explains a step.

blocks.title: Neutral or not?
blocks.q: Which sentence belongs in an expository report on recycling? (a) “Aluminum cans can be recycled and made into new cans.” (b) “Everyone who doesn’t recycle is lazy.”
steps: (a) states a fact a reader can check.
(b) is a judgment, and an unfair one: it doesn’t explain anything.
Expository writing keeps to facts and explanations.

blocks.title: Revise to inform
blocks.q: Revise for a report: “Volcanoes are super scary and totally awesome.”
steps: “Scary” and “awesome” are the writer’s feelings.
Replace them with information: what a volcano is or does.
blocks.a: “A volcano is an opening in Earth’s crust where melted rock, gas and ash escape.”

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Honeybees live in colonies of thousands of bees.
Bees are the coolest insects ever.
A worker bee’s job changes as it gets older.
It is silly to be afraid of bees.

blocks.cap: Sort the sentences for a report about bees.

items: Facts that can be checked: dates, sizes, amounts.
Definitions of terms the reader may not know.
Examples that make an idea concrete.
Steps in order, for how something works.
A neutral voice: no “amazing,” “terrible” or “you should.”

blocks.html: Slipping your own opinions into writing meant to inform (“the amazing,” “the worst,” “obviously”). Check every adjective and adverb: does it describe the subject, or your feelings about it? Keep the first kind; cut the second.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Expository Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Essay Writing

blocks.html: Expository writing can explain in several ways. Each way has a structure and signal words that tell the reader how the ideas relate.

head: Structure
It answers
Signal words
rows: is, means, is called, refers to
How does it happen or how is it done?
How are they alike and different?
Why does it happen? What results?
because, so, as a result, leads to
blocks.cap: Five ways to explain.

blocks.html: Explain by definition, classification, process, compare and contrast, or cause and effect. Choose the structure that answers your reader’s question, and use its signal words.
Each structure matches a question a reader might ask. Signal words tell them in advance what kind of answer is coming, so they know whether to look for steps, for differences or for reasons.

blocks.title: Name the structure
blocks.q: “Frogs and toads are both amphibians. However, frogs usually have smooth, damp skin, while toads have dry, bumpy skin.”
steps: Signal words: both, however, while.
It shows how two things are alike and how they differ.
blocks.a: Compare and contrast.

blocks.title: Match the question
blocks.q: A reader asks, “Why did the creek flood?” Which structure answers?
steps: “Why” asks for causes.
The answer will give causes and their effect: heavy rain, so the creek rose.
blocks.a: Cause and effect.

blocks.title: Classification
blocks.q: A paragraph begins: “Clouds come in three main types: cirrus, cumulus and stratus.” What structure will it use, and what will each sentence after it do?
steps: “Types” is a classification signal.
Each following sentence will describe one type and what sets it apart.
blocks.a: Classification: one type per sentence or group of sentences.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: First, the caterpillar forms a chrysalis. Then its body changes inside.
Unlike a moth, a butterfly usually rests with its wings folded up.
Because the pond froze, the ducks flew south early.
To make paper, workers mash wood into pulp, press it flat and dry it.
Both cats and lions are hunters, but only lions live in groups.
Heavy rain washed soil into the river, so the water turned brown.

blocks.cap: Sort each sentence by its structure. Look for the signal words.

blocks.html: Mixing structures in one paragraph without signal words, so the reader can’t tell whether they are reading steps, differences or causes. A longer piece may use several structures, but give each its own paragraph and its own signals.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Expository Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Transitional Devices

blocks.html: In I Think, Because you wrote an opinion with a reason. Expository writing sticks to facts. Before you write to persuade, you need to tell three kinds of statements apart.

head: Kind
What it is
Example
rows: can be checked and shown true or false
The library is open until 6 p.m. on weekdays.
The library is the best place in town.
a statement an argument sets out to prove with reasons and evidence
The library should stay open until 8 p.m. on weekdays.
blocks.cap: Facts, opinions and claims.

blocks.html: A fact can be checked. An opinion is a belief or judgment. A claim is a debatable statement that an argument supports with reasons and evidence. A false statement is still a statement of fact: it can be checked, and it fails.

Arguments are built from facts in support of claims. If you can’t tell which is which, you may think a strong feeling proves something, or that a fact you agree with settles a question it doesn’t touch. Sorting statements is the first step in judging any argument.

blocks.title: Words that signal judgment
blocks.q: Fact or opinion? “Summer is the most enjoyable season.”
steps: “Most enjoyable” is a judgment. People disagree, and no measurement settles it.
Words like best, worst, beautiful, boring and should often signal opinion.
blocks.a: Opinion.

blocks.title: A strongly worded statement
blocks.q: Fact or opinion? “It is absolutely certain that pizza is the greatest food.”
steps: Strong words (“absolutely certain”) don’t make something checkable.
“Greatest food” is still a judgment.
blocks.a: Opinion, however strongly it is stated.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Our school has 420 students.
Blue is the prettiest color.
The school should add a bike rack, because more students now ride.
cards.why: It takes a position and gives a reason, ready to be argued.

cards.text: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Homework is boring.
Our town should plant trees on Main Street.

blocks.cap: Sort the statements. A claim takes a position someone could argue for or against.

blocks.html: Treating a strongly worded opinion as a fact, or thinking a fact you agree with proves an opinion. Check: ask “How could someone test this?” If there is a way (count it, measure it, look it up), it is a statement of fact. If the answer depends on taste or values, it is an opinion.
Opinions are not bad. Informed opinions, backed by evidence, are what good arguments and the Debate section are made of. The point is to know when you are stating one.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argumentative Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Using Research and Evidence

blocks.html: Persuasive writing turns a claim into a case. It takes a position, gives reasons, backs each reason with evidence, and answers the other side fairly.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Our school should keep the library open after school until 5 p.m.
Many students have nowhere quiet to study at home.
In a survey of our seventh grade, 46 of 120 students said they have no quiet place to do homework.
An open library would give those students a calm place to work.
Some say the extra hours would cost too much, but parent volunteers have offered to help staff the desk.
A few more hours could help dozens of students do their best work.

blocks.cap: A persuasive paragraph: claim, reason, evidence, explanation, an answer to the other side, and a close (an invented school).

blocks.html: Persuasive writing takes a position and supports it with reasons and evidence. It answers the strongest objection fairly and asks the reader to agree or act.

Readers are persuaded by reasons they can check, not by volume. A writer who treats the other side fairly earns trust; one who mocks it loses readers who were still deciding. That is why good persuasion argues against the best version of the other view.

blocks.title: Opinion to argument
blocks.q: Strengthen: “Recess should be longer because recess is great.”
steps: The reason just repeats the opinion.
Find a real reason: students focus better after moving.
Add evidence: what the school’s teachers noticed, or a study from a reliable source.
blocks.a: “Recess should be longer because students focus better after they move; our teachers report calmer afternoons on days with a long recess.”

blocks.title: Make a case, not an attack
blocks.q: Which is better persuasive writing? (a) “People who want shorter recess don’t care about kids.” (b) “Shorter recess gives more class time, but the time is worth little if students can’t focus.”
steps: (a) attacks people instead of their reasons. That is the ad hominem fallacy.
(b) states the other side’s real reason, then answers it.

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: A persuasive essay grows from the same parts: reasons with evidence, then the other side.

blocks.html: Giving opinions without support, or attacking the other side instead of making a case. Check every reason: is there evidence under it? Check every mention of the other side: would someone who holds that view agree you described it fairly?

Persuasive writing and debate use the same moves. The Debate section’s chapters on building a case and steelman vs strawman practice them out loud, and the Logic Ladder names the fallacies to avoid. Rhetoric, the next course, turns this into the full argument essay.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argumentative Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argument Papers

blocks.html: A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph. A thesis statement does the same job for a whole essay. Whether you are persuading or explaining, the thesis tells the reader the one main point every paragraph will support.
A thesis states the essay’s main point or claim in a sentence or two, usually at the end of the introduction. It is a statement, not a topic, a question or a plain fact.

An essay without a thesis is a pile of paragraphs. The thesis gives the reader a reason to keep reading and a way to see how each paragraph fits. It also guides the writer: any paragraph that doesn’t support the thesis doesn’t belong.

head: Not a thesis
Why not
A thesis
rows: This essay is about the Civil War.
Railroads helped the Union win the Civil War by moving troops and supplies faster.
Middle schools should start at 8:30 or later so students get more sleep.
a plain fact: nothing to explain or prove
The Wright brothers succeeded because they tested every idea in their own wind tunnel.
blocks.cap: Turning non-theses into theses.

blocks.title: Topic to thesis
blocks.q: Turn the topic “school uniforms” into a thesis.
steps: Ask: what do I want to show about school uniforms?
Take a position or make a point: uniforms save families money.
Add the main reasons, if you like.
blocks.a: “School uniforms save families money and time, because one set of clothes replaces a closet of school outfits.”

blocks.title: Explaining, not arguing
blocks.q: Write a thesis for an expository essay on how honeybees make honey.
steps: An expository thesis states what the essay will explain.
Name the main stages.
blocks.a: “Honeybees make honey in three stages: they gather nectar, pass it between workers, and fan it until it thickens.”

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: The thesis sits at the end of the introduction, and each body paragraph supports it.

blocks.html: Writing a topic (“This essay is about the Civil War”), a question, or a plain fact as a thesis. Check: could a reader agree or disagree, or ask “how?” or “why?” If the sentence leaves nothing to explain or prove, it is not a thesis yet.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Creating a Thesis Statement, Thesis Statement Tips
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Developing Strong Thesis Statements

blocks.html: Every thesis states a main point. A strong thesis also gives the essay something worth doing, and something it can finish.

items: Specific: it names exactly what you will show, not a vague “good” or “bad.”
Arguable or worth explaining: a thoughtful reader could disagree, or would learn something.
Supportable: you can back it up with evidence in the space you have.

blocks.html: A strong thesis is specific, arguable (or worth explaining), and supportable in the length you have. Too broad, too obvious or too vague, and the essay has no clear job.

An obvious thesis (“Pollution is bad”) gives the reader no reason to read on. A vague one (“Social media has pros and cons”) can’t guide the paragraphs. A huge one can’t be proven in five paragraphs. Purdue OWL’s thesis guides make the same point: the thesis should take a position others might challenge, and be narrow enough to support.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Our town should add a crosswalk at Oak and Fifth, where three accidents happened last year.
Technology has changed the world.
Exercise is good for you.
Homework has advantages and disadvantages.
A four-day school week would hurt families who rely on school meals.
There are many interesting things about the ocean.

blocks.cap: Sort each thesis by its main strength or problem.

blocks.title: From vague to strong
blocks.q: Strengthen: “Video games have good and bad effects.”
steps: Vague: which effects? for whom?
Pick one specific, arguable point.
Make it supportable: one kind of game, one effect.
blocks.a: “Strategy games can improve planning skills, because players must think several moves ahead.”

blocks.title: From too broad to strong
blocks.q: Strengthen for a three-page essay: “World War II changed everything.”
steps: “Everything” can’t be supported in three pages.
Narrow to one change and one place.
blocks.a: “World War II opened factory jobs to American women, changing what many families expected women to do.”

blocks.html: Choosing a thesis too broad to support, or too obvious to need an essay. Check with two questions: Would anyone disagree, or learn something? Could I support it well in the pages I have? Both answers must be yes.

An arguable thesis is not the same as a controversial one. “Our library should open on Sundays” is arguable and calm. Strong writing takes a clear position on a question that matters to its readers, and supports it with care.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Developing Strong Thesis Statements
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Creating a Thesis Statement, Thesis Statement Tips

blocks.html: With a thesis in hand, plan the essay before you draft it. An outline lists the thesis, the main points and their support, in order.

head: Level
Outline
rows: Our school should start a composting program, because it cuts waste, teaches science and feeds the garden.
Food scraps make up a large share of our trash.
Students can measure how fast scraps break down.
Classes can study the worms and microbes at work.
Compost adds nutrients to the soil.
The garden would need less store-bought fertilizer.
blocks.cap: A short outline: Roman numerals for main points, capital letters for support.

blocks.html: An outline puts the thesis, the main points (I, II, III) and their support (A, B) in order. Each main point supports the thesis; each sub-point supports its main point.

An outline lets you see the whole essay at once, while it is still easy to change. Moving a line in an outline takes a second; moving a paragraph in a draft takes much longer. It also shows gaps: a main point with no support underneath needs more research.

blocks.title: Does each point fit?
blocks.q: A student adds “IV. Compost bins come in many colors.” to the outline above. Does it belong?
steps: Ask: does it support the thesis (cuts waste, teaches science, feeds the garden)?
The color of bins does none of those.
blocks.a: No. It doesn’t support the thesis, so it comes out.

blocks.title: Where does it go?
blocks.q: Where does “Students can test the soil before and after adding compost” fit?
steps: It is a science activity, but it is also about the garden.
It best supports II (teaches science), as a third sub-point C.
blocks.a: Under II, as C.

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: The five-paragraph essay as an outline.

blocks.html: Skipping the outline, or writing one whose points don’t each support the thesis. Check by reading the thesis, then each Roman numeral after it with “because” in between: “We should compost, because … composting teaches science.” If a line doesn’t make sense after “because,” it doesn’t support the thesis.
Outlines can be formal (numerals and letters) or quick lists. What matters is the order and the fit, not the format.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Research Papers: Where Do I Begin?
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Essay Writing

blocks.html: An outline gives you the essay’s plan. The introduction brings the reader in: it catches their interest, gives the context they need, and leads to the thesis.

items: A question the essay will answer: “What would you do with an extra hour of sleep?”
A short scene: “At 6:15 a.m., Maya’s alarm rings for the third time.”
A surprising fact, from a reliable source.
A brief quotation that fits the topic.

blocks.html: An introduction moves from a hook (a question, a scene, a surprising fact or a quotation) to the context the reader needs, to the thesis, usually its last sentence.
Readers decide quickly whether to keep reading. A specific hook gives them a reason to. The context then makes sure everyone, even a reader new to the subject, can follow the thesis when it arrives.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: At 6:15 a.m., Maya’s alarm rings for the third time, and she still can’t open her eyes.
Like many teenagers, she falls asleep late and must be at school by 7:30.
Sleep experts recommend eight to ten hours a night for teens, but many get far less.
Our district should move the high school start time to 8:30 a.m. so students can get the sleep they need.

blocks.cap: An introduction: hook, context, thesis.

blocks.title: Replace a weak opener
blocks.q: Improve: “Since the beginning of time, people have needed sleep.”
steps: “Since the beginning of time” is a sweeping claim no one can support, and it says nothing specific.
Replace it with something concrete about this topic: a scene, a question or a specific fact.
blocks.a: “At 6:15 a.m., Maya’s alarm rings for the third time.”

blocks.title: The dictionary opener
blocks.q: What is weak about “Webster’s dictionary defines sleep as a natural state of rest”?
steps: Every reader already knows what sleep is.
It uses up the first sentence on nothing new.
Define a word only when your reader needs the definition, and then in your own context.
blocks.a: It tells the reader nothing new and delays the point.

blocks.html: Opening with a dictionary definition or a sweeping claim (“Since the beginning of time…”, “In today’s society…”). Check your first sentence: could it begin a hundred different essays? If so, replace it with something that only fits yours.

Many writers draft the introduction last, once they know exactly what the essay says. The sleep figure in the example is the American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s recommendation for ages 13 to 18, as the CDC reports it; in your own essays, cite facts like this.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Essay Writing
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argumentative Essays

CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, “Short Sleep Duration Among Middle School and High School Students, United States, 2015” (teens 13–18: 8–10 hours, per the American Academy of Sleep Medicine)

blocks.html: After the introduction, the body of an essay does the work. Each body paragraph is a paragraph like the ones you built with supporting details, with one more job: it ties back to the thesis.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: A later start time would help students do better in class.
After Lakeview High moved its start to 8:30, most students in a school survey said they slept more and felt less tired in class.
Students who are awake can follow a lesson instead of fighting to keep their eyes open.
Rested students also have the patience to work through a hard problem.
Better sleep is not only about health; it is also about learning.

blocks.cap: A body paragraph: topic sentence, evidence, commentary, and a link onward (Lakeview High is invented).

blocks.html: A body paragraph has a topic sentence tied to the thesis, evidence, commentary that explains how the evidence supports the point, and often a link to what comes next.

Evidence doesn’t speak for itself. The reader needs you to say what the evidence shows and why it matters for your thesis. Purdue OWL’s guide to body paragraphs puts the explanation at the heart of the paragraph: the writer, not the source, makes the argument.

blocks.title: Add the commentary
blocks.q: Topic sentence: “Trees on Main Street would help local shops.” Evidence (invented for practice): “In a survey of shoppers, most said they would stay longer on a street with shade trees.” What comes next?
steps: Ask: so what? What does the study show about our street?
Link it to the claim: more time on the street means more time in the shops.
blocks.a: “If shoppers stay longer on a shady Main Street, they have more time to stop in and buy something.”

blocks.title: Tie it to the thesis
blocks.q: Thesis: “Our school should start a composting program.” Which topic sentence fits a body paragraph? (a) “Composting teaches science.” (b) “Worms are interesting animals.”
steps: (a) gives a reason for the program, so it supports the thesis.
(b) is about worms in general; it doesn’t say why the school should compost.

blocks.html: Dropping in evidence without explaining how it supports the point. Check each paragraph: after every piece of evidence, is there at least one sentence of your own that answers “so what?” If the paragraph ends on a quotation or a number, it is probably missing its commentary.
The school and the survey in these examples are invented for practice. In your essays, name and cite every study and survey you use.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Body Paragraphs (argument papers)
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), On Paragraphs

blocks.html: A concluding sentence closes one paragraph. A conclusion closes a whole essay, after the body paragraphs have made the case.
A conclusion returns to the thesis in new words, pulls the main points together, and shows why it matters: a larger meaning, a result or a next step. It doesn’t start a new argument.

The end of an essay is what the reader remembers best. A conclusion that only repeats the introduction wastes that moment. One that shows why the point matters gives the reader something to take with them.

items: So what? Why should the reader care?
What next? A step the reader, the school or the town could take.
The bigger picture: how the point connects to something larger.
Echo the hook: return to the opening scene or question, now answered.

blocks.title: Restate, don’t repeat
blocks.q: Thesis: “Our district should move the high school start time to 8:30 a.m. so students can get the sleep they need.” Write the first sentence of a conclusion.
steps: Keep the idea; change the words.
Fold in what the essay showed: health and learning.
blocks.a: “An 8:30 start would give students the rest that their health and their schoolwork depend on.”

blocks.title: Echo the hook
blocks.q: The essay opened with Maya’s 6:15 a.m. alarm. How could the conclusion end?
steps: Return to the scene, changed by the essay’s argument.
blocks.a: “With an 8:30 start, Maya’s alarm could ring once, and she could answer it.”

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: A few minutes of planning each night can turn a stressful week into a calm one.
In conclusion, this essay was about planning.
Also, many people think calendars should be paper.
cards.why: A new point at the end.

cards.text: If every student tried it for one week, the results would speak for themselves.

blocks.cap: Which sentences belong in a conclusion?

blocks.html: Avoid announcing the ending (“In conclusion, this essay showed…”). The reader can see the essay is ending. Spend those words on why the point matters instead. A short essay may need only three or four sentences of conclusion.

Repeating the introduction word for word, or starting a brand-new point. Check: compare your first and last paragraphs side by side. They should share an idea, not sentences. And every idea in the conclusion should already be in the essay.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argumentative Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Essay Writing

blocks.html: You now have all the parts: an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. The five-paragraph essay puts them in the simplest complete shape.

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: The five-paragraph essay. Switch to Outline to see it as a plan.

blocks.html: An introduction ending in a thesis, three body paragraphs (one main point each), and a conclusion. It is a starting form: it teaches how an essay holds together, and it fits timed tests and short assignments well.

The form makes the structure of an argument visible: one claim, several supports, each in its own place. Once you can build it reliably, you know what every essay needs. Purdue OWL’s guide to argumentative essays presents it the same way, as a common method, not the only one.

blocks.title: Build the plan
blocks.q: Plan a five-paragraph essay: “Every student should learn to cook.”
steps: Introduction: a hook (the cost of takeout), context, and the thesis.
Body 1: cooking saves money.
Body 2: cooking builds healthy habits.
Body 3: cooking teaches planning and math.
Conclusion: the thesis in new words, and a next step (a cooking elective).
blocks.a: Intro → money → health → skills → conclusion.

blocks.title: Spot the problem
blocks.q: A student’s body paragraphs are: “Cooking saves money.” “Cooking is cheaper than eating out.” “Cooking teaches planning.” What is wrong?
steps: The first two are the same point in different words.
So the essay has only two reasons, padded to look like three.
blocks.a: Two body paragraphs make the same point; merge them or find a real third reason.

blocks.html: Forcing every topic into exactly three points, even when it has two or five. Three is a habit, not a rule. Check: are your three points truly different, and is each one strong? If not, write two good body paragraphs, or four. The form serves the ideas, not the other way around.
Some teachers and tests expect five paragraphs; many college instructors do not. Learn it well, then learn to grow beyond it.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argumentative Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Essay Writing

blocks.html: The five-paragraph essay is scaffolding. As your subjects get harder, let the argument decide the shape: how many sections, in what order, and how long each one is.

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: The five-paragraph essay beside an argument that has grown.

blocks.html: Let the argument choose the number and order of paragraphs. A big reason may need three paragraphs; a small one may share one. Make room for the other side, and write a conclusion that does more than restate.

Real questions don’t come in threes. A writer who forces three points either pads a thin one or squeezes a big one. Longer essays also need things the basic form has no slot for: background, the strongest objection, a definition the argument depends on.

items: Sections instead of paragraphs: one main point may take several paragraphs.
Background: a paragraph of history or definitions before the argument.
The other side: a paragraph that states the strongest objection fairly and answers it.
Order by logic: put the point the others depend on first.
A conclusion with a job: what follows, what to do, what is still open.

blocks.title: Two reasons, one objection
blocks.q: An essay argues that the town should build a skate park. The writer has two strong reasons (safety and a place for teens to meet) and one serious objection (cost). Plan it.
steps: Introduction with the thesis.
Safety: two paragraphs, because it has the most evidence.
A place for teens: one paragraph.
The cost objection, stated fairly, then answered (grants, shared costs).
Conclusion: what the town gains, and a next step.
blocks.a: Six paragraphs, shaped by the reasons, not by a formula.

blocks.title: Choose the order
blocks.q: Point A: “The creek floods every spring.” Point B: “Building houses on the floodplain would put families at risk.” Which comes first?
steps: B depends on A: the risk only makes sense once the reader knows about the flooding.
Put the point the others rest on first.
blocks.a: A, then B.

blocks.html: Treating the five-paragraph form as the definition of an essay, so the writing can’t grow with harder subjects. Check your plan: does each section exist because the argument needs it, or because the form has a slot?
The argument essay in the Rhetoric course builds on this, with counterarguments, concessions and the Toulmin model. Debate cases grow the same way: see the Debate section’s case builder.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argumentative Essays
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Argument Papers

blocks.html: In Body Paragraphs you learned that every point needs evidence. Not all evidence is the same. Each kind has strengths and limits, and a good writer chooses the kind that fits the claim.

head: Kind
Example
Strength
Limit
rows: may not prove a bigger point alone
72% of surveyed students walk to school.
depends on who was counted and how
Last winter the north lot flooded twice.
A pediatrician explains why teens need sleep.
only as good as the expert’s field and evidence
My cousin got sick after swimming in the lake.
one story can’t prove a general claim
blocks.cap: Five kinds of evidence.

blocks.html: Facts, statistics, examples, expert testimony and anecdotes can all support a point. Match the evidence to the claim: a general claim (“most,” “usually,” “students”) needs evidence about many cases, not one story.

Evidence earns a reader’s trust only if it fits what it is asked to prove. One vivid story can make a reader feel something, but it can’t show that something is common. Purdue OWL’s guide to research and evidence makes the same point: use reliable, relevant evidence, and say how it supports your claim.

blocks.title: Name the kind
blocks.q: “According to the National Weather Service, lightning can strike more than ten miles from a storm.”
steps: It reports what an expert source says.
The source is a government weather agency with the knowledge to say it.
blocks.a: Expert testimony (from an authoritative source).

blocks.title: Does it fit the claim?
blocks.q: Claim: “Most students in our school want a later start time.” Evidence: “My friend Ava says she would love to sleep in.” Is that enough?
steps: The claim is about most students: a general claim.
The evidence is one person’s view: an anecdote.
A general claim needs evidence about many people, such as a survey of the school.
blocks.a: No. One anecdote can’t show what most students want.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: In our class survey, 18 of 25 students said they read before bed.
A park ranger explains that feeding ducks bread can harm them.
My uncle says he never wears a seat belt and has always been fine.
cards.why: One person’s story, and it can’t outweigh evidence about many drivers.

cards.text: The bridge on Route 9 closed twice last spring for repairs.

blocks.cap: Sort each piece of evidence by its kind.

blocks.html: Treating one story, an anecdote, as proof of a general claim. Logicians call it a hasty generalization. Check: count the cases behind your evidence. If the claim says “most” or “people,” the evidence should cover many people, not one.

Anecdotes still have a place: they make a statistic human. Pair them: “72% of surveyed students walk to school; for Sam, that walk is two miles each way.” Debaters weigh evidence the same way; see the Debate section’s chapter on research and evidence.

blocks.html: A quotation is one kind of evidence: the exact words of a source. You know the punctuation from Quotation Marks and Dialogue. Here is how to use a quotation well in an essay.

items: Introduce it with a signal phrase: who said it, and why they matter.
Quote exactly, in quotation marks. Use an ellipsis (…) for words you leave out and square brackets for a word you change, and never change the meaning.
Cite it: the author and page, in the style your class uses.
Explain it: after the quotation, say what it shows and how it supports your point.

blocks.html: Introduce the quotation, quote the words exactly, cite the source, and explain what the quotation shows. A quotation is a piece of evidence, not a replacement for your own words.

A quotation that appears out of nowhere leaves the reader asking who said it and why it is there. The signal phrase answers the first question; your explanation answers the second. Quote only when the exact words matter: they are vivid, authoritative, or the very thing you are discussing.

blocks.name: wr-mark

sentences.text: Getting enough sleep may help students remember what they learn.
In a study of middle school students, the researcher Maria Delgado found that “students who slept nine hours recalled more of the previous day’s lesson” (205).
If sleep helps memory, a later bedtime may cost students more than rest: it may cost them what they studied.

blocks.cap: A signal phrase introduces the quotation, and commentary explains it. (Delgado is an invented practice source.)

blocks.title: From dropped to introduced
blocks.q: Improve: “Sleep matters. ‘Students who slept nine hours recalled more of the previous day’s lesson’ (Delgado 205).”
steps: The quotation is dropped in with no introduction.
Add a signal phrase: who is speaking, and their role.
Add a sentence of explanation after it.
blocks.a: “The researcher Maria Delgado found that ‘students who slept nine hours recalled more of the previous day’s lesson’ (205). Sleep, in other words, helps students keep what they learn.”

blocks.title: Fair or unfair trimming?
blocks.q: Original: “The new park is popular, but it is not safe after dark.” A writer quotes: “The new park is … safe after dark.” Is that allowed?
steps: The ellipsis removed “popular, but it is not.”
The quotation now says the opposite of the original.
An ellipsis may shorten a quotation, never change its meaning.
blocks.a: No. It reverses the meaning, which misquotes the source.

blocks.html: Dropping a quotation in with no introduction, or ending a paragraph on a quotation without explaining it. Check: before each quotation, is there a signal phrase? After it, is there at least one sentence of your own? The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Quoting, Paraphrasing, and Summarizing
Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), MLA In-Text Citations: The Basics

blocks.html: Quotations borrow a source’s exact words. Often you need only its main ideas. A summary gives those ideas in your own words, much more briefly.
A summary states a source’s main ideas in your own words, much shorter than the original, in the source’s order of importance, without your opinions. It still needs a citation.

Summaries let you bring a whole article into one sentence of your essay, so the reader gets the point without reading the source. Leaving out your opinion keeps the summary fair: the reader can trust that it reports the source, not you.

items: Read the whole source, then look away from it.
Ask: what is the author’s main point? What are the two or three key supports?
Write those in your own words.
Check against the source: is anything wrong or missing? Cite it.

blocks.name: wr-compare

opts.original: City parks do more than give people a place to play. Trees in a park cool the air around them on hot days, which can make nearby streets several degrees cooler. Parks also soak up rainwater that would otherwise rush into storm drains, and they give birds and insects a place to live in the middle of the city. For these reasons, many planners now treat parks as part of a city’s basic equipment, like roads and pipes.

versions.label: Summary A
versions.text: Parks help cities in practical ways: they cool the air, absorb rain and shelter wildlife, so planners now count them as basic equipment.

versions.label: Summary B
versions.text: Parks are great and every city should build more, because I love going to the park on weekends.
versions.note: This gives the writer’s opinion and leaves out the source’s points.

versions.label: Summary C
versions.text: City parks do more than give people a place to play. Trees in a park cool the air around them on hot days. Parks also soak up rainwater.
versions.note: This copies sentences and follows every detail instead of the main idea.

blocks.cap: Judge each summary. The marks show words copied from the original.

blocks.title: Cut to the main idea
blocks.q: Summarize in one sentence: a five-paragraph article explains that octopuses can open jars, escape tanks, recognize individual people and use coconut shells as shelters.
steps: What do the examples have in common? They show intelligence.
Main idea: octopuses are clever problem-solvers.
Name the kinds of evidence briefly, not every one.
blocks.a: “The article argues that octopuses are clever problem-solvers, citing their skill with jars, tanks, tools and even human faces.”

blocks.html: Name the source as you summarize, so the reader knows whose ideas these are: “In her article on city parks, the author argues that…” A summary of a short article might be one or two sentences; a summary of a book, a paragraph or two.

Retelling every detail in order, or adding what you think of the source (“which is very interesting”). Check: is your summary much shorter than the original? Does every sentence report the source, not you?

Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Plagiarism FAQs

blocks.html: A summary shrinks a whole source. A paraphrase restates one passage in your own words and your own sentence structure, at about the same length, so you can use its details.

blocks.name: wr-compare

opts.original: Honeybees tell each other where flowers are by dancing: the angle of the dance shows the direction, and its length shows the distance.
opts.source: Reyes and Brandt, “Why Bees Dance” (an invented practice source)

versions.label: Version A
versions.text: Honeybees inform one another where blossoms are by dancing: the angle of the dance indicates the direction, and its length shows the distance.
versions.note: Only a few words were swapped; the structure is the source’s.

versions.label: Version B
versions.text: A bee that finds food reports its location with a dance; the dance’s angle points the way, and how long it lasts signals how far to fly (Reyes and Brandt 22).

blocks.cap: Copied runs of words are marked. Judge each version.

blocks.html: A fair paraphrase changes both the words and the sentence structure, keeps the meaning exactly, and cites the source. Swapping a few synonyms is not enough.

A writer’s sentences are their work, just as the ideas are. If you keep the shape of someone’s sentence and change a few words, you are still borrowing their writing. Purdue OWL calls a paraphrase “your own rendition of essential information and ideas” expressed in a new form; writing teachers call the too-close version patchwriting.

items: Read the passage until you understand it.
Cover it, and write the idea as you would explain it to a friend.
Compare: did you keep the meaning? Did any phrase of three or more words slip in unchanged? Rewrite it, or quote it.
Add the citation.

blocks.title: Paraphrase a sentence
blocks.q: Original: “Students who slept nine hours recalled more of the previous day’s lesson.” (Delgado 205)
steps: The idea: more sleep, better memory of yesterday’s lesson.
New structure: start with the lesson, or with memory.
Cite it.
blocks.a: “The longer students slept, the more they remembered of what they had learned the day before (Delgado 205).”

blocks.html: Swapping in a few synonyms but keeping the source’s sentence structure (patchwriting). That still borrows the author’s writing, and it counts as plagiarism. Check by laying your version beside the original: if the sentences line up phrase by phrase, start again from the idea, not the words.

The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up. Some phrases have no good substitute, like a name or a technical term (“chlorophyll”). Keep those; the rest should be yours.

sources.name: Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), Paraphrase: Write It in Your Own Words

blocks.html: Quoting, summarizing and paraphrasing all use someone else’s work. Plagiarism is using another person’s words or ideas without giving them credit, whether on purpose or by accident.

head: You use
Quotation marks?
Citation?
rows: Their idea, data, chart or image
blocks.cap: When to give credit.

blocks.html: Put a source’s exact words in quotation marks, and cite anything you quote, paraphrase or summarize, including ideas, numbers and images. Common knowledge needs no citation. When in doubt, cite.

Citations do three jobs: they give credit to the people whose work you used, they let your reader check and follow up, and they show which ideas are yours. Purdue OWL describes common knowledge as information a reader can find in many credible sources (it suggests about five as a rough guide), and its golden rule is “When in doubt, just cite.”

blocks.title: Common knowledge or not?
blocks.q: Does “George Washington was the first president of the United States” need a citation? Does “About one in four teens in the survey reported fewer than six hours of sleep”?
steps: The first is in countless reliable sources and known to most readers: common knowledge.
The second is a specific finding from one survey: someone did the work to find it.
blocks.a: The first, no. The second, yes.

blocks.title: A paraphrase needs credit too
blocks.q: Lucas rewrites a paragraph from a website entirely in his own words and leaves out the source. Is that plagiarism?
steps: The words are his, but the ideas came from the website.
Ideas need credit as well as words.
blocks.a: Yes. A paraphrase still needs a citation.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: A quotation from a scientist’s article.
Water freezes at 0 °C.
cards.why: Common knowledge, found in any science book.

cards.text: A summary of a magazine story.
A chart you copied from a government report.
Your memory of your first day at a new school.
An argument you first read in a blog post, in your own words.
cards.why: The idea came from someone else.

blocks.cap: Which uses need a citation?

blocks.html: Thinking a citation is needed only for direct quotations, or that facts everyone knows need one. Ideas, paraphrases, summaries, numbers and images all need credit; common knowledge doesn’t. Check: did I learn this from a particular source while working on this paper? If yes, cite it.
Accidental plagiarism usually starts with careless notes. When you take notes, put copied words in quotation marks and write the source and page beside every note, so you always know what is yours.

blocks.html: Good evidence comes from good sources. Anyone can publish online, so before you trust a source, check it.

head: Ask
Look for
rows: an author or organization with real knowledge of the subject
data, named sources, links you can follow
a date recent enough for the topic
to inform, or to sell, persuade or entertain?
the same facts in independent, reliable sources
blocks.cap: Five questions for any source.

blocks.html: Judge a source by its author, its evidence, its date, its purpose, and whether other good sources agree. A source that is clear about who made it and where its facts came from earns more trust.

Your essay is only as reliable as its sources. A reader who finds one weak source starts to doubt the rest. Purdue OWL’s guides to evaluating sources ask the same kinds of questions: the author’s background, the date, the evidence, and the purpose or bias.

blocks.title: Compare two sources
blocks.q: For a report on how much sleep teens need: (a) a CDC report that cites the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, or (b) a mattress company’s blog post. Which is stronger?
steps: (a) comes from a public health agency and names its expert source.
(b) comes from a company that sells mattresses: its purpose is to sell.
The blog may be right, but you would want to confirm it elsewhere.
blocks.a: (a), the CDC report.

blocks.title: Is the date a problem?
blocks.q: A 2009 article lists “the newest phones.” A 2009 article explains how the heart pumps blood. Which date matters more?
steps: Phones change every year, so a 2009 list is out of date.
How the heart works hasn’t changed.
blocks.a: The date matters for the phone article, much less for the heart article.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: The author is named, with their training or job.
The page has no author, no date and no sources.
Facts link to the studies they came from.
Every paragraph ends with a “Buy now” button.
Two independent, reliable sources report the same numbers.
It has a professional design and was the first search result.
cards.why: Neither looks nor search rank shows accuracy.

blocks.cap: Sort the signs.

blocks.html: Trusting a source because it looks professional or came first in a search. Design and search rank don’t show accuracy. Check by leaving the page: search for the author and the organization, and look for the same facts in another reliable source.
Encyclopedias are good places to start and to find sources, but cite the sources they lead you to when you can. On this site we use primary and official sources first.

blocks.html: Research starts with a topic you have narrowed and sources you can trust. The next step is a research question: a focused question that several good sources together can answer.

head: Too broad
A fact to look up
A research question
rows: How deep is the Pacific Ocean?
How does plastic in the ocean affect sea turtles?
How many hours do teens sleep?
How does screen time before bed affect how teens sleep?
When was the Golden Gate Bridge built?
Why are some bridges built as suspension bridges and others as arch bridges?
blocks.cap: Turning topics and facts into research questions.

blocks.html: A good research question is focused, can’t be answered with one fact, and needs several sources to answer well. Take notes that record where each idea came from.

A question gives research a direction: you know what to look for and when you have enough. A one-fact question ends with one search; a good research question leads you to compare sources, which is where real understanding begins.

blocks.title: Sharpen the question
blocks.q: Improve: “What about recycling?”
steps: Too vague: what about it?
Narrow to one part and ask how or why.
Make sure several sources could help answer it.
blocks.a: “Why do some towns stop recycling glass, and what happens to the glass instead?”

blocks.title: A note that keeps its source
blocks.q: What should a research note include?
steps: The idea, in your own words, or the exact words in quotation marks.
The source: author and title, or a short label that matches your source list.
The page or section.
blocks.a: “Glass is heavy, so shipping it far costs more than it earns (Liu, ‘Glass’ 4).”

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: How tall is Mount Everest?
How has climbing Mount Everest changed since the 1950s?
What year did the first email get sent?
How did email change the way offices work?

blocks.cap: Which questions need research from several sources?

blocks.html: Searching for one fact instead of asking a question that needs several sources to answer. Check: could one search result answer it in a sentence? If so, ask how or why about it.

items: Write the question at the top of your notes.
Find three or more reliable sources.
Note each idea with its source and page.
Revise the question if your research shows a better one.
