blocks.html: You know why to give credit from Avoiding Plagiarism. A citation style is an agreed format for giving it, so every reader knows where to look. Three styles are common in American schools.

head: Style
Current edition
Used mostly in
In the text
rows: numbered notes, with a bibliography (or an author-date system)
blocks.cap: Three citation styles and their current editions.

blocks.html: MLA 9 (2021) for literature and the humanities; APA 7 (2020) for psychology and the social sciences; Chicago 18 (2024) for history and publishing. Use the style your teacher or publisher asks for, in its current edition, and only one style per paper.

Each field cites what its readers care about. Social scientists want to know how recent a study is, so APA puts the date up front. Literature scholars quote page by page, so MLA puts the page in the text. Historians often discuss their sources in notes, so Chicago gives them footnotes.

blocks.name: wr-cite
blocks.cap: One invented practice book in all three styles. Same facts, different order and punctuation.

blocks.title: Which style?
blocks.q: A student writes a psychology report on memory. Which style is most likely?
steps: Psychology is a social science.
APA is the American Psychological Association’s style.
blocks.a: APA (7th edition).

blocks.title: Which edition?
blocks.q: A website teaches MLA rules “from the 8th edition (2016).” Is that current?
steps: The current MLA Handbook is the 9th edition, from April 2021.
Most rules carried over, but some details changed.
blocks.a: No. Check the rule against MLA 9.

blocks.html: Mixing styles in one paper (an MLA works-cited list with APA dates in the text), or following an older edition’s rules. Check: name your style and edition at the start, and use one guide for it, such as Purdue OWL’s pages, which follow the current editions.
Editions change slowly: MLA 9 came out in 2021, APA 7 in 2019 (dated 2020) and Chicago 18 in 2024. Each style’s official website posts updates between editions.

blocks.html: MLA, from Citation Styles and Their Uses, lists sources on a Works Cited page. MLA 9 builds every entry from the same core elements, in the same order, so one pattern works for books, articles and websites. Titles follow Titles: Italics or Quotation Marks.

head: Core element
Ends with
blocks.cap: MLA 9’s core elements, in order. Skip any that don’t apply.

blocks.html: An MLA entry: author, title of the source, then the container that holds it (a journal, a website, a book of essays) with its details. A whole book is italicized; a piece inside a container goes in quotation marks, and the container is italicized.

The container idea lets one pattern cover anything: an article sits in a journal, a page sits in a website, a song sits in an album. The reader can always find the piece by first finding its container.

blocks.name: wr-cite
blocks.cap: A journal article (an invented practice source): the article’s title in quotation marks, the journal in italics.

blocks.title: A book
blocks.q: Build the entry: author Ellen Marsh; book The Quiet Garden: Growing Food in Small Spaces; publisher Larkspur Press; 2019.
steps: Author, last name first: Marsh, Ellen.
A book stands alone, so its title is italicized.
No container. Publisher, then date.
blocks.a: Marsh, Ellen. The Quiet Garden: Growing Food in Small Spaces. Larkspur Press, 2019.

blocks.title: A web page
blocks.q: Build the entry: Grace Liu, “How to Start a Neighborhood Library,” on the website Open Shelf Guide, 4 May 2023, at www.openshelfguide.example/neighborhood-library.
steps: The page is inside a website: title in quotation marks.
The website is the container: italicized.
Date in day-month-year order, with the month abbreviated; then the location (URL without https://).
blocks.a: Liu, Grace. “How to Start a Neighborhood Library.” Open Shelf Guide, 4 May 2023, www.openshelfguide.example/neighborhood-library.

blocks.html: Leaving out the container (the website, journal or book that holds the piece), or italicizing the article’s title instead of the container’s. Check: is the thing you cite part of something bigger? Then it gets quotation marks, and the bigger thing gets italics. The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up.

The Works Cited page is alphabetized by the first word of each entry, double-spaced, with a hanging indent (lines after the first indented half an inch). For a DOI, MLA 9 uses the full link, https://doi.org/….

Purdue Online Writing Lab (Purdue OWL), MLA: Changes in the 9th Edition (released April 2021)

blocks.html: Every Works Cited entry has a partner in the text: a short in-text citation that points the reader to it. MLA uses the author’s last name and the page number.

head: Case
In-text citation
rows: Marsh argues that small gardens can feed a family (42).
blocks.cap: MLA 9 in-text citations. Every source named here is invented for practice.

blocks.html: An MLA in-text citation gives the author’s last name and the page, with no comma and no “p.”: (Marsh 42). It usually goes at the end of the sentence, before the period. The name must match the first word of a Works Cited entry.

The in-text citation is short so it doesn’t interrupt the reading, and exact so the reader can find both the entry and the page. Starting with the same word as the Works Cited entry makes the match instant.

blocks.name: wr-cite
blocks.cap: An MLA in-text citation: author and page.

blocks.title: Place it
blocks.q: Add the citation (Delgado, page 205) to: Students who slept nine hours remembered more.
steps: Author’s last name and page, no comma: (Delgado 205).
Put it before the final period.
blocks.a: Students who slept nine hours remembered more (Delgado 205).

blocks.title: With a signal phrase
blocks.q: Rewrite with the author named in the sentence.
steps: The name is in the sentence, so the parentheses hold only the page.
blocks.a: Delgado found that students who slept nine hours remembered more (205).

blocks.html: Adding a comma or “p.” inside the parentheses, as in (Delgado, p. 205). Those belong to other styles (APA uses both). Check MLA by its pattern: name, space, number: (Delgado 205).

For a quotation that ends with a question mark or an exclamation point, keep that mark inside the quotation and add a period after the citation. The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up.

blocks.html: APA, introduced in Citation Styles and Their Uses, puts the date near the front, because in the sciences how recent a study is matters. APA 7 calls its list References.

head: Part
APA 7 pattern
rows: (Reyes & Brandt, 2020); in a sentence: Reyes and Brandt (2020)
(Kim et al., 2021), from the first citation
sentence case: Sleep and memory in middle school students
title case, italic: Journal of Student Health, 14(3)
blocks.cap: APA 7 patterns. Every source named here is invented for practice.

blocks.html: APA cites by author and date: (Lee, 2020, p. 12) in the text, and reference entries that begin Lee, A. B. (2020). Titles of articles and books use sentence case; journal names use title case and italics.
In fields that build on new research, the year tells a reader at once whether a finding is fresh or has been tested by later work. Sentence case keeps long scientific titles easy to read.

blocks.name: wr-cite
blocks.cap: An APA reference for a journal article: sentence-case title, italic journal and volume, issue in parentheses, DOI as a link.

blocks.title: A book reference
blocks.q: Build the APA reference: Ellen Marsh, The Quiet Garden: Growing Food in Small Spaces, Larkspur Press, 2019.
steps: Author: Marsh, E.
Date in parentheses: (2019).
Title in italics and sentence case: capitalize the first word, the first word after the colon, and proper nouns.
Publisher.
blocks.a: Marsh, E. (2019). The quiet garden: Growing food in small spaces. Larkspur Press.

blocks.title: An in-text citation with a quotation
blocks.q: Cite a quotation from page 205 of Delgado’s 2022 article.
steps: Author, year, page with p., separated by commas.
blocks.a: (Delgado, 2022, p. 205)

blocks.html: Capitalizing every word of an article or book title in an APA reference. APA uses sentence case there: only the first word, the first word after a colon, and proper nouns. (Journal names keep title case.) Check each capital in a title: is it one of those three? The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up.
APA 7 lists up to 20 authors in a reference, uses “et al.” in the text for three or more authors from the first citation, and gives DOIs as links (https://doi.org/…). It also endorses singular they.

blocks.html: Chicago, from Citation Styles and Their Uses, offers two systems. Its notes and bibliography system, common in history and the arts, puts a small number in the text1 and the source in a numbered footnote (or endnote), with a bibliography at the end. Its author-date system works much like APA.

head: Kind
Example (an invented practice book)
rows: 1. Ellen Marsh, The Quiet Garden: Growing Food in Small Spaces (Larkspur Press, 2019), 42.
Marsh, Ellen. The Quiet Garden: Growing Food in Small Spaces. Larkspur Press, 2019.
blocks.cap: Chicago 18 notes and bibliography.

blocks.html: A note gives the source in reading order (First Last, Title (Publisher, year), page). Later notes are shortened: last name, short title, page. The bibliography inverts the first author’s name and uses periods. The 18th edition prefers shortened notes to ibid.

Notes let a writer cite and comment on sources without interrupting the main text, which suits history, where sources are discussed in detail. Shortened notes are clearer than ibid. (“in the same place”): the reader sees the source’s name at once instead of hunting back through earlier notes.

blocks.name: wr-cite
blocks.cap: A first note for a book.

blocks.title: Note to bibliography
blocks.q: Turn the note “Maria Delgado, “Sleep and Memory in Middle School Students,” Journal of Student Health 14, no. 3 (2022): 205.” into a bibliography entry.
steps: Invert the name: Delgado, Maria.
Periods between main parts instead of commas.
Give the article’s full page range instead of one page: 201–19 (Chicago shortens the second number).
blocks.a: Delgado, Maria. “Sleep and Memory in Middle School Students.” Journal of Student Health 14, no. 3 (2022): 201–19.

blocks.title: Ibid. or a short note?
blocks.q: Note 4 cites Marsh, page 42. Note 5 cites Marsh again, page 60. What should note 5 say?
steps: Ibid. would work, since note 4 is the same source, but Chicago 18 discourages it.
The preferred form is the shortened note.
blocks.a: 5. Marsh, Quiet Garden, 60.

blocks.html: Using Ibid. everywhere. The 18th edition prefers shortened notes and discourages ibid., which can only ever point to the source of the note just before. If a note for another source comes between, ibid. would point to the wrong one.

Other Chicago 18 changes: the place of publication is no longer needed for books published after 1900, and a bibliography entry lists up to six authors before “et al.” Chicago 18 also accepts singular they. The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up.

blocks.html: You have built citations in MLA, APA and Chicago. Reading them matters just as much: a citation in someone else’s list is a map to a source you may need.

blocks.name: wr-cite
blocks.cap: One journal article (invented) in three styles. The colors mark the same parts in each.

blocks.html: Every citation holds the same parts: author, title of the source, container (journal, website or book), volume and issue, publisher, date, pages and location (DOI or URL). Styles change the order and punctuation, not the parts.

To find a source, you need its container first: the library or database lists journals, not single articles. Knowing which part is which lets you search the right name and check that a citation is complete.

head: Clue
Part it marks
rows: Quotation marks around a title (MLA, Chicago)
the title of a source inside a container
the pages of the whole article
blocks.cap: Clues to the parts.

blocks.title: Title or container?
blocks.q: In “Reyes, Thomas, and Anna K. Brandt. “Why Bees Dance: Signals in the Hive.” Field Biology Review, vol. 8, no. 1, 2020, pp. 15-34.”, which is the journal?
steps: The title in quotation marks is the article.
The italic title after it is the container.
blocks.a: Field Biology Review is the journal (the container).

blocks.title: Read an APA reference
blocks.q: In “Delgado, M. (2022). Sleep and memory in middle school students. Journal of Student Health, 14(3), 201–219.”, what is 14? What is 3?
steps: After the italic journal name comes the volume, also italic: 14.
The issue follows in parentheses, not italic: 3.
blocks.a: Volume 14, issue 3.

blocks.html: Confusing the title of an article with the title of the journal or website that published it. Check the typeface: in MLA, APA and Chicago, the container is italicized; the article is not. The sources in these examples are invented for practice: the authors, titles and publishers are made up.

blocks.html: In The Writing Process you met revising: changing what a draft says and how it is organized. Now that you can build a whole essay, from thesis to conclusion, you can revise one.

head: Move
Example
rows: an example where a point has no support
a paragraph that drifts from the thesis
the strongest reason to the end; the background before the argument
a vague sentence with a specific one; a weak example with a strong one
blocks.cap: The four moves of revision.

blocks.html: Revise by adding, cutting, moving and replacing. Work from big to small: the thesis first, then the support, then the order, then clarity. Fix sentences last, when you are editing.

Big problems hide small ones and make them pointless to fix: polishing a paragraph you later cut is wasted work. Starting with the thesis and the order makes sure the essay is worth polishing before you polish it.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.ins: Students who move during the day pay attention better in class.
segments.why: Replace: a reason that supports the claim, not a feeling.

segments: Our teachers notice calmer afternoons after long recesses.

segments.why: Cut: true, but it doesn’t support the point.

segments.ins: A longer recess would help students learn.
segments.why: Add: a closing sentence that returns to the claim.

blocks.cap: Three revisions with their reasons. Switch between Changes, Before and After.

blocks.title: Revise for order
blocks.q: An essay arguing for a school garden has its paragraphs in this order: (1) the garden teaches science, (2) what a school garden is and how one works, (3) the garden provides fresh food. What should move?
steps: Paragraph 2 is background: readers need it before the reasons.
Move it right after the introduction.
blocks.a: Background first: 2, then 1 and 3.

blocks.title: Revise for support
blocks.q: A body paragraph says, “Bike lanes make streets safer. Everyone knows this. Bike lanes are good.” What does it need?
steps: “Everyone knows this” and “Bike lanes are good” add no support.
Add evidence: a fact, statistic or example from a reliable source, with commentary.
blocks.a: Replace the two empty sentences with evidence and an explanation.

blocks.name: wr-checklist
blocks.cap: A revision checklist. Tap to check items off, or print it.

blocks.html: Only fixing sentences, and never asking whether a paragraph belongs or is in the right place. Check by outlining your finished draft: write each paragraph’s point in a few words. Does the list follow from the thesis, in a sensible order? That reverse outline shows what to move, cut or add.
Let a draft rest for a day if you can. Time away lets you read it more like a stranger would.

blocks.html: You can revise on your own, but another reader sees what you can’t: the gap you filled in with what you meant. Giving and using feedback well is a skill of its own.

items: Specific: point to the exact place: “the second paragraph,” “this sentence.”
Kind: about the writing, not the writer.
Actionable: something the writer can try.
Balanced: name what works, then one or two things to try.

blocks.html: Useful feedback is specific, kind and actionable: name what works, then suggest one or two things to try. When you receive it, listen, ask questions, and decide what to use; it is still your writing.

Vague praise (“Good job!”) feels nice but teaches nothing. Vague criticism (“This is confusing”) leaves the writer guessing what to fix. Specific comments show the writer exactly what a reader experienced, and that is what they need to revise.

head: Vague
Specific and actionable
rows: Your opening question made me want to keep reading.
In paragraph 3, I couldn’t tell whether “they” meant the students or the teachers.
Could you add an example of a time the bus was late?
The last paragraph adds a new reason. Could it return to your thesis instead?
blocks.cap: From vague to useful.

blocks.title: Make it useful
blocks.q: Improve this comment on a classmate’s essay: “Your evidence is weak.”
steps: Where? Name the paragraph or the claim.
Why? Say what a reader needs.
What to try? Offer one idea.
blocks.a: “In paragraph 2, the only support is your cousin’s story. A survey or a fact from a reliable source would make the claim stronger.”

blocks.title: Using feedback
blocks.q: Two readers disagree: one says to cut your opening story, the other loved it. What do you do?
steps: Ask each reader why.
Check the story against your purpose: does it lead to the thesis?
You decide; feedback is information, not orders.
blocks.a: Find out why, test it against your purpose, then decide.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Nice!
The dialogue in the first scene sounds like real people talking.
It needs work.
Your thesis says three reasons, but I found only two body paragraphs.

blocks.cap: Sort the comments.

blocks.html: Giving vague praise or vague criticism instead of a specific suggestion. Check each comment: does it point to a place, say what you noticed, and suggest something to try? If not, add the missing piece.

blocks.html: After revising, editing makes every sentence correct: grammar, punctuation, spelling and format. You know the rules from Usage and Mechanics, such as Five Ways to Fix a Run-On. The challenge is seeing your own errors.
Edit for grammar, punctuation, spelling and format, one kind of error at a time. Read slowly and aloud, or on paper, so you see what you wrote and not what you meant.

Your brain knows what you meant to write, so it fills in missing words and fixes typos as you read your own work at normal speed. Slowing down, reading aloud, or changing how the page looks breaks that habit and lets the real words through.

items: Read aloud, slowly, pointing at each word.
Print it, or change the font or size, so it looks new.
Make one pass for each kind of error you tend to make.
Read the last sentence first, then the one before it, to check sentences one at a time.
Use spell check, then check what it can’t catch: their/there, its/it’s, a missing word.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: A sound-alike word: our shows belonging.
A run-on: two sentences need a period between them.
Spelling: a lot is two words.

blocks.cap: Edit one error at a time; each edit shows its reason.

blocks.title: What spell check misses
blocks.q: Spell check found nothing wrong in “Its time to feed the dog it’s dinner.” Find the errors.
steps: “Its time” means “it is time”: it’s.
“it’s dinner” means “its dinner,” the dog’s dinner: its.
Both words are real words, so spell check can’t tell.
blocks.a: “It’s time to feed the dog its dinner.”

blocks.title: The missing word
blocks.q: Find the error: “We went to the the library after school.”
steps: Read it aloud, one word at a time.
The word “the” appears twice; at reading speed, eyes skip the repeat.
blocks.a: “We went to the library after school.”

blocks.name: wr-checklist
blocks.cap: An editing checklist to tap or print.

blocks.html: Proofreading on screen at reading speed, so your eyes fill in what you meant to write. Check by changing how you read: aloud, on paper, or backward sentence by sentence.

blocks.html: One part of revising is cutting. Wordy writing uses many words where a few would say the same thing, and every extra word makes the reader work harder.

head: Wordy
Concise
rows: in spite of the fact that
blocks.cap: Wordy phrases and their concise forms.

blocks.html: Cut words that add nothing: empty phrases (“due to the fact that” → “because”), repeats (“blue in color” → “blue”), and buried verbs (“made a decision” → “decided”). Keep every word that tells the reader something.

Strunk’s rule 13 (1918) begins: “Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.” He adds that this means not that every sentence be short, “but that every word tell.”

blocks.name: wr-revise

opts.before: Due to the fact that it was raining, we made the decision to stay inside.
opts.after: Because it was raining, we decided to stay inside.

blocks.cap: Step through the cuts.

blocks.title: Cut the empty phrase
blocks.q: Revise: “In my opinion, I think that the library should be open on Sundays.”
steps: “In my opinion” and “I think” say the same thing. Keep one.
“That” can often go too.
blocks.a: “I think the library should be open on Sundays.” (Or, stronger: “The library should be open on Sundays.”)

blocks.title: Free the buried verb
blocks.q: Revise: “The committee came to the conclusion that the park needs more benches.”
steps: The real action is hiding in a noun: conclusion.
Turn it back into a verb: concluded.
blocks.a: “The committee concluded that the park needs more benches.”

blocks.html: Padding writing to reach a word count, which makes it harder to read. If you need more words, add more content: another example, a clearer explanation, the other side’s view. Check each sentence: what does each word do? If you can cut a word without losing meaning, cut it.
Concise doesn’t mean short or choppy. A long sentence full of useful detail is concise; a short one with an empty phrase is not. Concision in the Rhetoric course goes further.

blocks.html: You learned the parts of a friendly letter in First Writing. A formal letter (also called a business letter) has a different audience: someone you may not know, often at a business, a school office or a city department.

blocks.name: wr-note
blocks.cap: A formal letter in block format, with each part labeled.

head: Part
What goes there
rows: your street, city, state and ZIP (skip it on letterhead)
the reader’s name, title, organization and address
Dear Ms. Bennett: (a colon is traditional in a formal letter)
the purpose first, then details, then what you are asking for
your handwritten signature above your typed name
blocks.cap: The parts of a formal letter, top to bottom.

blocks.html: A formal letter has your address, the date, the inside address, a salutation, the body, a closing and a signature. In block format every line starts at the left margin, with a blank line between parts and paragraphs.

A formal letter may be filed, forwarded or answered weeks later by someone else. The inside address and the date make it a complete record; the clear purpose in the first lines lets a busy reader act on it. A respectful tone gives the request its best chance.

blocks.title: Friendly or formal?
blocks.q: Fix the closing and salutation for a letter to the city parks director: “Hi Mr. Grant, … Love, Sam”
steps: “Hi” and “Love” suit a friend, not an official.
Use “Dear Mr. Grant:” and “Sincerely,”.
blocks.a: “Dear Mr. Grant:” … “Sincerely, Sam Ortiz”

blocks.title: Purpose first
blocks.q: Which first sentence is better for a letter asking to use the library’s meeting room? (a) “My name is Maya and I like to read.” (b) “I am writing to ask whether our writing club could use the community room on Saturday, April 26.”
steps: (b) states the request at once.
(a) delays it; the reader doesn’t yet know why you wrote.

blocks.html: Using a friendly letter’s tone and closing (“Love,” “See ya”) in a formal letter, or leaving out the inside address. Check the top and bottom of the page: both addresses and the date at the top; a formal closing, a signature and your typed name at the bottom.
Purdue OWL notes that a comma after the salutation is used with “open punctuation”; the colon is the traditional formal choice. The letter in the picture is invented.

blocks.html: An email to a teacher, a coach or a business is a short formal letter that arrives instantly. It has fewer parts, but the same need for a clear purpose and a respectful tone.

blocks.name: wr-note
blocks.cap: A clear email, with its parts labeled.

blocks.html: A clear email has a specific subject line, a greeting, the main point first, short paragraphs, a polite closing and your name. Read it once more before you send it.

People decide whether and when to open an email from its subject line, and many read only the first lines on a phone. A request at the top gets answered; a request buried at the end gets missed. Purdue OWL’s email guide gives the same advice: a subject that sums up the message, and a message that is concise and polite.

blocks.title: Write the subject line
blocks.q: You need to ask Ms. Ruiz whether you can turn in your history essay a day late because you were sick. Write a subject line.
steps: Not blank, and not just “Question” or “Hi.”
Name the topic and the request in a few words.
blocks.a: “Request: one-day extension on history essay”

blocks.title: Main point first
blocks.q: Reorder: (1) “Thank you for your time.” (2) “I was home sick on Monday and Tuesday.” (3) “Could I turn in my history essay on Thursday instead of Wednesday?”
steps: The request (3) goes first, so it can’t be missed.
Then the reason (2).
Then the thanks (1).

blocks.name: wr-note
blocks.cap: Put the parts of the email in order, then Check.

blocks.html: Burying the request at the end, or leaving the subject line blank. Check before you press Send: does the subject line say what the email is about? Would the reader know what you are asking after the first two sentences?

items: Use a school or plain, sensible address.
Greet the reader by name and title: “Dear Ms. Ruiz,” or “Hello Ms. Ruiz,”.
Skip emoji, slang and all capitals in a formal email.
Proofread: an email can’t be unsent.
